Lesson 2 · Technical continuation

Distributions and association

The same stores, calculation, and decision—with the specification and reproducible steps visible.

Baseline · weeks 1–8 · one average per store

← Return to the worked analysis

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

Use the same analysis rows

The baseline profile is an average of eight weekly percentages for each store. Equal monitoring exposure and equal weeks give every store the same weight in the overall average.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Group mean = sum of store baseline rates divided by stores in the group. Above-target share = count(baseline_rate > 10) divided by that group’s store count. Quantiles are calculated across store averages, not across all weekly rows.

stores = world()['stores']
worked_mean = stores.baseline_rate.mean()
summary = stores.groupby('risk_group').baseline_rate.agg(['count','mean','median'])
above = stores.assign(above=stores.baseline_rate > 10).groupby('risk_group').above.mean()
assert np.isclose(worked_mean, lesson_result(2)['mean'])

# Inspect distribution and association using the same store profiles.
stores = world()['stores']
rates = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy()
counts, edges = np.histogram(rates, bins=np.arange(0, 36, 4))
assert counts.sum() == 150
sample_sd = rates.std(ddof=1)
correlation = np.corrcoef(stores.baseline_demand, rates)[0,1]
assert np.isclose(sample_sd, lesson_result(2)['depth']['sd'])
assert np.isclose(correlation, lesson_result(2)['depth']['correlation'])
x = stores.baseline_demand.to_numpy()
products = (x-x.mean()) * (rates-rates.mean())
covariance = products.sum() / (len(x)-1)
assert np.isclose(covariance, np.cov(x,rates,ddof=1)[0,1])
assert np.isclose(correlation, covariance/(x.std(ddof=1)*sample_sd))
# Recalculate distributions and association within each group.
group_checks = {}
for name, g in stores.groupby('risk_group'):
    q = g.baseline_rate.quantile([.25,.5,.75])
    corr = g.baseline_demand.corr(g.baseline_rate)
    group_checks[name] = dict(n=len(g),quartiles=q.to_list(),r=corr)
    bands = pd.cut(g.baseline_rate, [-np.inf,10,15,np.inf])
    shares = bands.value_counts(sort=False) / len(g)
    assert np.isclose(shares.sum(), 1)
assert sum(g['n'] for g in group_checks.values()) == 150
# Verify normalization and the relation between raw and binned views.
for width in [2,4]:
    edges = np.arange(4,24+width,width)
    counts, _ = np.histogram(rates, edges)
    density = counts / (len(rates)*width)
    assert counts.sum() == len(rates)
    assert np.isclose((density*np.diff(edges)).sum(), 1)
binned = stores.assign(bin=pd.qcut(stores.baseline_demand,5))
bin_means = binned.groupby('bin',observed=True).baseline_rate.mean()
assert np.isclose(bin_means.mean(), rates.mean())

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

These are descriptive summaries of the complete baseline release. They do not require a sampling interval to describe that release. Uncertainty about a new audit or future outcomes is introduced separately in Lessons 3 and 6.

Change one analytical choice

Change the service target to 12% or 15% and recalculate group coverage. Explain how the operational review workload changes even though the underlying distribution stays fixed.

Probability and measurement extend the descriptive toolkit

A sample space lists outcomes and an event selects a subset

  • Outcome ω: one possible result
  • Sample space Ω: all possible results
  • Event A: a set of outcomes
  • P(Ω) = 1; P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A)

For a product-day availability check, the sample space can be {available, unavailable}. The stockout event selects unavailable. A random variable maps each outcome to a number: X equals one for unavailable and zero otherwise. Distinguish the outcome, the event, and the numerical variable before assigning probabilities.

Discrete probabilities add; continuous densities contribute area

  • Discrete: finitely many or countably infinite possible values
  • Probability mass: p(x) ≥ 0 and Σp(x) = 1
  • Continuous density: f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1
  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx for a continuous variable

A count can have infinitely many possible integer values and remain discrete. For an absolutely continuous model, interval probabilities are areas and any single point has probability zero. A density height can exceed one because the area, not the height, is the probability. Empirical frequencies describe observed rows; a probability model describes possible repetitions.

Subtract the intersection when adding event probabilities

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

The union means A or B or both, and the intersection means both. Adding event probabilities counts the intersection twice, so subtract it once. Mutually exclusive events have an empty intersection and therefore zero overlap. For example, mutually exclusive stockout bands form a partition of stores whose shares add to one.

Conditioning changes the denominator; independence preserves the probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B); independence: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)

Conditional probability uses B as the restricted denominator, provided P(B)>0. Under independence, learning B leaves P(A) unchanged. Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities cannot be independent: observing one makes the other impossible. Independence permits simultaneous occurrence with a product probability.

Bayes combines a prior probability with new evidence

P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A) / [P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | Aᶜ)P(Aᶜ)]

Bayes reverses the direction of conditioning by combining a prior with likelihoods. Illustrative planning example: suppose 20% of stores are high risk; a flag appears for 80% of high-risk stores and 10% of other stores. Among 100 stores, expect 16 flagged high-risk and 8 flagged others. The high-risk share among flagged stores is 16/(16+8)=2/3. These probabilities illustrate Bayes and are not fitted results from the case. The denominator must be positive.

Expected values and variances weight outcomes by their probabilities

μ = E[X] = Σₓ x p(x); Var(X) = Σₓ (x − μ)²p(x); SD(X) = √Var(X)

For an illustrative count with values 0, 1, and 2 and probabilities 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2, the expectation is 0.7. The weighted squared deviations are 0.5×0.49 + 0.3×0.09 + 0.2×1.69 = 0.61, so SD is about 0.781. These are population probability moments and use no n−1 correction. Continuous models replace the sums by integrals when the moments exist.

Joint probabilities determine conditional means and covariance

E[Y | X=x] = Σᵧ y p(y | x); Cov(X,Y) = ΣₓΣᵧ (x−μₓ)(y−μᵧ)p(x,y)

A joint distribution assigns probability to pairs. Divide p(x,y) by p(x)>0 to get p(y|x), then average Y using those conditional probabilities. Covariance weights paired deviations by the joint probabilities. The empirical calculation gives every observed pair equal weight; the sample version additionally uses the n−1 normalization. For continuous pairs, use joint and conditional densities and integrals.

Bernoulli and binomial models describe indicators and counts

Indicator and count models
ModelSupport and probabilityMean; variance
Bernoulli(p)0 or 1; P(X=1)=pp; p(1−p)
Binomial(n,p)k=0,…,n; C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏnp; np(1−p)

A Bernoulli model describes one binary opportunity with 0≤p≤1. A binomial model sums n independent Bernoulli opportunities with the same p; n is a nonnegative integer. C(n,k)=n!/[k!(n−k)!] counts the arrangements with k successes. A stockout count fits this model only when the specified opportunity structure matches those assumptions; the formulas explain the model itself.

Uniform and normal models specify different continuous shapes

Continuous distributions and their parameters
ModelParameters and supportMean; variance
Uniform(a,b)a<b; a≤x≤b; density 1/(b−a)(a+b)/2; (b−a)²/12
Normal(μ,σ²)σ>0; all real xμ; σ²

Uniform density is flat on a bounded interval: intervals of equal length have equal probability. Normal density is symmetric and bell-shaped, with location μ and scale σ. Its density is exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ√(2π)). Standard deviation is the square root of each listed variance. Specify support along with the shape to decide whether the model can describe the variable.

Lognormal and Pareto models describe positive right tails

Positive distributions; Pareto moments require α>1 and α>2 respectively
ModelSupport and definitionMean; variance
Lognormal(μ,σ²)x>0; log X ~ Normal(μ,σ²)exp(μ+σ²/2); (exp(σ²)−1)exp(2μ+σ²)
Pareto(xₘ,α)x≥xₘ>0; α>0; F(x)=1−(xₘ/x)ᵅαxₘ/(α−1); αxₘ²/[(α−1)²(α−2)]

The lognormal parameters describe log X, not the level mean and SD. The Pareto formula uses scale xₘ and shape α consistently: its mean is finite only for α>1 and its variance only for α>2. Its survival probability (xₘ/x)^α illustrates a power-law tail. Take the square root of variance for SD. This corrects the mixed Pareto parameterization in the original slides.

Standardize aligned proxies before constructing a composite score

zᵢⱼ = (proxyᵢⱼ − meanⱼ)/SDⱼ; compositeᵢ = Σⱼ wⱼzᵢⱼ, with Σⱼwⱼ = 1

A latent concept, such as operating capability, is not directly observed. A proxy is a recorded indicator intended to measure part of it. Choose one defensible proxy or combine several. For a composite, align directions so larger scores always mean the same thing, standardize measures on a stated reference sample, and declare the weights. A zero-variance proxy cannot be standardized. A common 1–5 scorecard can instead average aligned items on their existing common scale.

Illustrative example: a standardized replenishment-discipline score of 1 and a standardized record-accuracy score of −0.5 give an equal-weight composite of 0.25. The index makes a measurement choice explicit; it does not establish that the latent concept has been measured without error.

Principal components summarize variation through data-chosen weights

  • Start with aligned, usually standardized indicators
  • The first component maximizes variance of a linear combination
  • Later components summarize remaining orthogonal directions
  • Inspect loadings and give the resulting score a substantive meaning

Principal component analysis (PCA) chooses weights from the indicator covariance or correlation matrix. The first loading vector has unit length and maximizes the variance of the resulting score. Later components are orthogonal and capture remaining variation. PCA weights need not be positive or sum to one, and their overall sign is arbitrary. It is an optional way to reduce dimension, not a guarantee that the largest-variance direction is the business concept of interest.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

All 150 store profiles are calculated from the same eight repaired weekly records per store. The group comparison introduces no new dataset and changes no stockout definition.
